en: If your towering Choro should recover,
Would I not sever the fated thread,
Would I not begin the upheaval?
Saying, “Choro has seized Kyyaz,”
I would begin the struggle,
I would make my fame known.
My belly boils, my heart burns—
Such is the state you see me in.
My strength is spent, my vigor gone—
I am as one already dead.
I, once an eagle, have become earth;
I, once a lion—alas, my head—
Have become a dug black grave:
Such is the state you find me in.
If you call this living, I count among no living men;
I am as one already dead.
Bring that dead soul back to life,
Show me your power as my sister-in-law.
While my mighty elder lived,
I was a keen warrior who scattered foes.
A bullet struck and pierced my chest,
And I cannot turn about.
My arm is broken, my leg disabled,
And I cannot rise to my feet.
Abandoned to the enemy’s scorn,
I cannot stand tall.
Carrying firewood on my back,
Fallen among a wrathful people,
I cannot show my face.
Karagul has become our master;
At his shout, we lose our peace.
My moon-bright sister Aichürök,
You have cast great turmoil among men.
Do not let your thoughts be divided;
Do not let them call him a stranger’s son,
The child born from your own body.
The seething Jediger—
Let me bring their proud banner down.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh—
If my strength and power suffice,
Let me thrust his head into a pit.
If battle begins, let me do this:
Let me search every saddlebag
Of that sprawling swine;
Let me reap his grain while still green.
If fortune favors me, Kyyaz
I shall drive before me and torment.
Striking his mares out on the plain,
Let me smash his brains,
Take his camels as plunder,
And neatly slaughter his giant.
While splitting his belly like a donkey’s,
May my mind stay fixed upon the fool,
Until somehow I sever his head.
The man I fought was brave Kyyaz;
The man I sent flying was Semetey.
The one I must battle is Kanchoro;
The one I lost was Semetey.
My thoughts stray, sister-in-law,
To the torment suffered in humiliation.
My grief is vast, my anguish fierce:
May I die fighting.
I value my blood less than a spoonful;
For my khan and uncle, the gray-maned lion,
I shall spill every spoonful of my blood,
And spare my life not at all.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh—
If only I might somehow beat the fury from him;
The Jediger who fill the Seven Valleys—
If only I might drive them all away;
If only I might slaughter their champions!
I have words to speak in tears,
A vengeance that will never leave my heart.
If I clash with him and raise a battle,
May that sprawling dog and I
Fall together where no one sees us.
For him she braided her hair in sorrow;
After long delay, she finally saw him.
When the figure before her
Came into view, her heart was content:
He was the gift she had longed for
From the gray-maned hero who had died.
The spring flowing down the hillside,
The young hero left by the magnanimous lord,
The banner held within her hand,
The precious legacy she had received
From the banner-winning hero.
Born after his mother came as plunder,
He would cast the whole world into tumult.
The time had come when God fulfilled her wish.
The moon waned and the days passed;
Many years went by.
Living out her days in grief,
Drinking water through a reed,
Brave Seytek had grown up in suffering:
The time had come when God fulfilled her wish.
This very year your young hero
Had reached the age of twelve.
Calling the Seven Valleys his homeland,
Separated from broad Talas,
Leaving wooded Talas behind,
Leaving the joyous Kyrgyz people,
Plundered and plunged into grief,
The ill-fated young hero, still in the womb,
Was bereft of his father
And fled to make the Seven Valleys his home.
Separated from his father,
He drew strength from his mother Aichürök;
That dear land of the Seven Valleys
He fittingly made his home,
And the Jediger of the Seven Valleys
He fittingly made his people.
Despised, he nevertheless prospered;
Fatherless, he grew to manhood;
Battered, he nevertheless came of age,
And ninety beasts were slaughtered for his feast.
I have made my sorrow into song—
Hear my lament, Aichürök!
Let me open my eyes and behold him;
Let me open my mouth and kiss him;
Bring me your only son!
If your only child is a true champion,
I shall bind him at my waist as my support
And pursue the blood-price of the hero!
Smashing down their lattice walls,
Your young hero shall raise an uproar
And make their brides and maidens weep.
Let me cast hell among their throng;
If God lets me see that day,
As Kanchoro struts in his fullness,
I shall tear out his lungs and take his gall,
And beat the ancient fury from him.
For my dear mother Kanykey,
For my mother in her old age,
And for the heroic lord Bakay,
Let me strike one sacrificial blow!
Let me gouge out his glaring eyes
And drive him all the way from Talas!
The black blood within him
I shall suck down and drink my fill!”
So spoke Külchoro,
And wrath seized him;
Not a hair’s breadth of strength remained
In the ruined wretch,
Whose heart held countless regrets.
Before he could finish speaking,
In the blink of an eye,
Before anyone could say another word,
She darted away like a doe;
The luckless woman’s
Agility revealed itself.
Shaking off her troubled thoughts,
She ran to the white palace,
And when she brought the child,
The spring flowing from the valley,
The young hero she had borne amid death,
He bristled like a tiger,
Raged like a wild boar,
And charged like the wind.
Look at his swaggering lionhood,
Inherited from father and forefather;
See what a lion he was!
The spring flowing from the terrace,
The young hero born to surpass
His father, the gray-maned warrior—
His aunt took him by the hand
And led him toward Choro,
Who stood there lamenting.
She brought him in like a prince who ruled a people.
His ear matched his father’s ear,
As though cast from the same mold;
His nose matched his father’s nose,
As though fashioned in its likeness;
His very scalp matched his father’s scalp,
As though one had been fitted over the other.
Broad-mouthed and cliff-browed,
His upper lip jutted wide
Like a Kalmyk’s bag.
His lashes were flame, his eyes were embers;
No mortal ever held such wonder.
His beauty was singular, his gaze direct;
Among the multitude, his speech was forthright.
His brows were dense as thickets;
The formidable pale boy
Looked able to swallow alive anyone who grappled with him.
He was like a champion who ruled a nation;
God Most High fashions
His servants in every manner.
If he gathered himself and sprang,
He looked ready truly to conquer the foe.
His brow was high, his menace fierce;
He would flatten anyone who challenged him.
Seeing the boy’s valor,
Abandon hope of a peaceful end.
His stature and bearing were extraordinary;
From afar, he looked like a mountain.
He had been named Seytek,
And from his mother’s words he learned
That his people were the Kyrgyz,
That renowned Talas was their land,
And that the Kyrgyz who inhabited Talas
Had never lost it to a disputing foe,
Never yielded their companion to another,
And were a people unlike all others.
He heard that Üch-Koshoy, Talas, and broad Chatkal
Were their lands;
He heard that the dear folk dwelling there
Were his people.
When stirred, they hunted deer;
When they were not weary, they simply
Played freely at their ease.
He heard that those dear folk, the nation’s mainstay,
Were his people;
He heard that patterned carpets and ten kinds of cloth
Adorned their tethering lines.
He heard that Ala-Too, fairest of lands,
Was their mountain,
And that the fruit of this Ala-Too—
Aichürök, the woman taken as spoil—
Was his mother.
He heard the black giant’s account
That his people were Kyrgyz;
He heard the rough giant’s words
That he was fashioned differently.
The hero Manas was his grandfather,
And Semetey his own father.
He heard that in hilly Talas, in broad Keñ-Kol,
His village stood.
Never sated no matter how much he drank,
Never abandoning his ravenous desire,
When ridden through darkness
He prowled like a leopard;
Entered in a shooting contest, he brought good fortune;
Launched into battle, he equaled countless troops;
Once roused, he never missed his mark,
And none he struck survived.
Toward Külchoro’s side
She took the narrow shortcut,
Saying, “Pale-gray falcon, so full of spirit,
Well-born morning star,
Black-browed goshawk,”
And when she brought into the house
The young hero she had borne amid death,
Seytek, son of brave Semetey,
Was the very image of the gray-maned lion;
More than the hero himself,
He resembled the dark pupil of his eye.
He was like a prince who ruled a nation,
As though one scalp
Had been fitted over another,
As though the gray-maned lion had been born anew
And clothed in this form.
His front teeth gleamed white,
Like a chisel forged to shape stone;
When the boy charged,
He was a calamity to enemy warriors.
